title: Prediction market odds on Tesla-SpaceX merger are above 50% for early 2027
description: Tesla CEO Elon Musk during a state dinner in the East Room of the White House in Washington, Sept. 24, 2026.Annabelle Gordon | Bloomberg | Getty Image
body: Tesla CEO Elon Musk during a state dinner in the East Room of the White House in Washington, Sept. 24, 2026.Annabelle Gordon | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesFollowing a Barclays note Wednesday that outlined what a merger between Tesla and SpaceX could look like, prediction market traders increased the odds of an integration above 50% for early 2027.Odds of a merger happening before March jumped to 56% by Friday morning, up from 29%. Odds for an integration before April and May climbed to similar levels. The contract asks, "When will Tesla and SpaceX merge?" and will be verified by news outlets and the Securities and Exchange Commission's EDGAR database. Tesla, known for its electric vehicles, and SpaceX, a rocket and satellite company, have collaborated before. Both are controlled by Elon Musk. On Thursday, Tesla showed off its long-delayed Roadster, which relies on SpaceX technology to make the vehicle hover. A video showcasing the Roadster's capabilities was also recorded from SpaceX's test site in Texas.Beyond collaboration, the growing speculation of a merger comes after Musk spoke of "more and more overlap" between Tesla and SpaceX on the EV maker's latest earnings call. Barclays now expects a merger could be announced before Tesla's annual general meeting, which must take place no later than Dec. 6, 2026. Analyst Dan Levy expects the merger may be proposed as an AI vertical integration, involving Tesla's Robotaxi and Optimus with SpaceX's Grok and Macrohard. Terafab, the semiconductor project relying on Tesla, SpaceX and xAI, could also be a "key driver" for the merger, Levy added. "Notably, while we suspect there would be some financial synergies, the true value would be in vertical integration," Levy said. Earlier Friday, Evercore ISI recommended buying SpaceX shares ahead of its next scheduled earnings release, set for early November, and boosted its 12-month price target on the stock by 20% to $275.Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Prediction market odds on Tesla-SpaceX merger are above 50% for early 2027

title: U.S. presses China on Mastercard, Citigroup market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says
description: A Citibank branch in New York, US, on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBANGKOK – U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market
body: A Citibank branch in New York, US, on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBANGKOK – U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market access issues for Mastercard Inc and Citigroup Inc during at least two bilateral meetings with Chinese counterparts in Bangkok this week, according to a U.S. Treasury official. The Treasury delegation, led by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke, held bilateral meetings with officials from the People's Bank of China and the finance ministry on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance meetings and the IMF-World Bank annual gathering this week, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door meetings.The talks included market access for U.S. companies, including Mastercard, Visa and Citigroup, the official said, adding that regulatory approval was part of the agreement reached during the meeting between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping during the latter's state visit in Washington last month.The sideline meetings in Bangkok continued discussions on implementing these deals, the official said. The PBOC, China's National Financial Regulatory Administration, China Securities Regulatory Commission, Chinese embassies in Singapore and Thailand, the U.S. Treasury Department press office and Visa did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Citigroup and Mastercard declined to comment.The progress follows China's Oct. 13 approval for Visa Inc. to begin preparing a wholly owned domestic card-clearing business. Visa has up to a year to prepare before it applies for an operating license, the PBOC has said.China has opened much of its financial sector to foreign firms since 2018, gradually lifting foreign ownership caps on services such as securities, futures and fund management. It still limits cross-border capital flows and has kept state-backed domestic players dominant in payments. Mastercard currently operates yuan card payments in China through a local joint venture with NetsUnion Clearing Corp., which began operating in 2024. The pending approval would allow it to operate as an independent entity, the person said. Citigroup — which has hired several dozen employees for its China unit — is seeking a wholly owned securities license to conduct A-share brokerage, underwriting, research and principal trading businesses in the onshore market, two people familiar with the industry said, requesting anonymity for discussing private matters. One of the two people close to Citigroup said the bank planned to increase its China securities staff to about 100. The bank applied in late 2021, and Reuters reported last month that approval could come soon. Trump and Xi are expected to meet in person for the third time this year in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November. "The move suggests the US-China trade environment remains benign, and Beijing is keen to keep up the momentum," said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group. Licensing U.S. financial firms is a "limited concession" on market access, she said, though it signals China is continuing to open up, and "this should marginally bolster investor confidence in Chinese assets."

schema.headline: U.S. presses China on Mastercard, Citigroup market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says

title: Trump says he won't use nuclear weapons or send ground troops to Iran
description: U.S. President Donald Trump arrives to speak during a luncheon in the Rose Garden of the White House on Oct. 15, 2026 in Washington, DC. Kevin Dietsch
body: U.S. President Donald Trump arrives to speak during a luncheon in the Rose Garden of the White House on Oct. 15, 2026 in Washington, DC. Kevin Dietsch | Getty ImagesU.S. President Donald Trump has said he does not intend to use nuclear weapons against Iran or foresee deploying ground troops in the country.Speaking in an interview with Newsmax, broadcast Thursday evening, he said: "I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to. We're the greatest nuclear power in the world."The right-wing cable outlet asked Trump about reports that Washington was considering using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, or MOAB, widely known as the "Mother of All Bombs.""The mother of all bombs is not nuclear. It's not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb. It's like a tiny nuclear bomb. But the mother of all bombs is one big bomb, but it's not nuclear," he said, without specifically confirming or denying the reports.When asked if he would put "troops on the ground," Trump said: "No, I don't see that, I don't see it."The MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal. It was used in combat in 2017 against ISIS militants in Afghanistan.MOAB strike plansEarlier on Thursday, CNN reported that the U.S. military has developed new strike plans to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.The strikes could take place if Trump orders combat operations to resume, either before or after the midterm elections, the outlet reported. The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.Trump said on Oct. 8 that he would not order a resumption of military strikes before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.Hormuz attack riskMerchant shipping through the Strait of Hormuz faces heightened risks after a series of attacks in the critical waterway.The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said that the threat remains "severe" in the Strait of Hormuz, after the Singapore-registered container ship GFS Pride was struck by an unknown projectile, caught fire and later sank.The UKMTO added that "deliberate hostile action" was highly likely and said it had recorded eight attacks in the critical waterway since Oct. 11.

schema.headline: Trump says he won't use nuclear weapons or send ground troops to Iran

title: Brent oil touches $110 as Iran escalates Hormuz attacks, Ukraine vows to hit Russian refineries
description: watch nowCrude oil prices rose sharply Friday as Iran escalated attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi militants fired missiles at Saudi Arabia and U
body: watch nowCrude oil prices rose sharply Friday as Iran escalated attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi militants fired missiles at Saudi Arabia and Ukraine vowed to keep striking Russian refineries. Brent futures hit a session high of $110 per barrel for the first time since May before easing slightly to close at $109.86, a gain of 3.7%.U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.5% to settle at $101.41 per barrel. WTI added more than 10% this week while Brent advanced nearly 5%.Saudi Arabia intercepted several missiles fired over the Red Sea on Friday, including one that was heading toward the oil export terminal Yanbu, a military spokesman said. Three drones were also destroyed in the kingdom's Riyadh and southern regions, the military said. Iran-allied Houthi militants in Yemen have repeatedly fired at Saudi Arabia this week. Oil giant Aramco came under attack when one of its administrative buildings in Dhahran was hit Tuesday, the kingdom's energy ministry said. The Houthis attacked Riyadh's international airport on Oct. 10, killing 12 and injuring more than 300.In the Strait of Hormuz, at least nine tankers and cargo ships have come under attack since Sunday as Iran tries to choke off oil exports through the waterway. Iran sank the container ship GFS Pride on Wednesday,  U.S. Central Command said. The crew of the Singapore-registered ship was safely evacuated, according to Singapore's maritime authority. The attacks have left three seafarers injured and two missing this week, according to the International Maritime Organization.Crude exports through Hormuz have pulled back after touching prewar levels in September. Shipments  stood at 9.4 million barrels per day for the week ended Wednesday, about 70% of the average before the Iran war, according to data provided by the energy researcher Kpler. Meanwhile, the "energy ceasefire" that President Donald Trump tried to broker between Ukraine and Russia has quickly unraveled. The Kremlin continued attacking Ukrainian infrastructure despite the supposed truce. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv would resume strikes on Russian refineries in retaliation.Diesel prices have surged this year due to Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries and Iranian strikes on energy infrastructure in the Middle East. The fuel cost an average of $6.33 a gallon in the U.S. Friday, more than 70% above the same period last year, according to AAA data. U.S. crude oil prices were also driven higher by a big decline of more than 8 million barrels for the week ended Oct. 9 in commercial inventories due to production shut-ins on the Gulf Coast from Hurricane Isaias, according to the Energy Information Administration.

schema.headline: Brent oil touches $110 as Iran escalates Hormuz attacks, Ukraine vows to hit Russian refineries

title: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge
description: A "For Sale" sign outside a single-family home in Carlsbad, California, U.S., Sept. 16, 2026. Mike Blake | ReutersLong-term bond yields above 5% and a
body: A "For Sale" sign outside a single-family home in Carlsbad, California, U.S., Sept. 16, 2026. Mike Blake | ReutersLong-term bond yields above 5% and a $2 trillion deficit are giving Americans a taste of what a U.S. debt crisis would be like. A true emergency would hurt much more, and isn't baked in. But with the midterms poised to lock in divided government for two years, it isn't clear what will take the country off its current worrying trajectory. Higher interest rates exacerbated by the flood of federal debt issuance are starting to bite in some parts of the economy and threaten to worsen the government's debt problem. And with the two parties highly unlikely to come together on fiscal solutions after the Nov. 3 midterms, any fixes are years off in the future. The housing market is showing signs of slowing as the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hovers around 7.5%. Pending home sales fell 4% in September, Redfin said Monday, the biggest monthly drop in three years. Mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield. The 10-year has climbed 114 basis points, or hundredths of a percentage point, since the end of February through midday Friday, when the 10-year traded at 5.1%.Several factors are pushing up the 10-year, including the war with Iran, which kicked off on Feb. 28 and precipitated the rise in long-term yields. Oil and diesel prices are up sharply, and that has bond traders asking for more yield to account for the possibility that central banks such as the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates. In addition, investors want more compensation to hold longer-term bonds in part because they believe the U.S. government will continue to flood the market with them. The markets for corporate and government debt are connected, and the competition for capital among them is intensifying as companies issue hundreds of billions in new debt to build the infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Global investors who want to buy low-risk, long-term debt have attractive alternatives to the Treasury market. If the U.S. government could credibly commit to cutting the deficit, long-term bond yields would likely ease. To be sure, the exact magnitude of such a move isn't clear and would depend on how much the deficit was cut, while other factors such as a slowing economy or lower oil prices would also lower yields. But the possibility of a virtuous cycle of lower deficits and lower yields is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued that the U.S. ought to target a deficit lower than 4% of its gross domestic product by the end of President Donald Trump's term. There is almost no way the U.S. will hit that target. The deficit was $1.992 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year, up 12% from last year, data released Friday by the U.S. Treasury showed. That deficit amounts to approximately 6.2% of gross domestic product, based on an estimate of third-quarter GDP. Higher rates make debt reduction tougher. If interest rates stay a half-point above the CBO's expectations, the cumulative deficit over 10 years will come in $1.9 trillion higher, the agency estimates. If rates overshoot by 1.5 points, that adds $6 trillion in deficits. The CBO expects the 10-year Treasury to average 4.3% over that period, compared with 5.1% today. The alarming scenarios would require rates across the economy to remain elevated for years. "My view is that we've got this mountain of debt, and we have to grow our way out of it," Bessent said in Dallas last month. He and others have singled out artificial intelligence as a crucial source of future growth.AI could help but can't fix the problem entirely. It would take a decade of 7.2% growth to balance the budget with growth alone, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a research group that advocates for balanced budgets. GDP growth was recently revised up for the second quarter from 1.5% to 2.2% at an annualized rate. The acceleration that quickly would get us to 7.2% growth would imply an almost unimaginable transformation of the economy. Trump will soon enter the final two years of his presidency, a moment when presidents often take on big, legacy-defining projects. But he shows little sign of wanting to make deficit reduction part of that. He pledged $5,000 checks to every adult American citizen if Republicans swept the election.In practice, Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House and possibly also the Senate. Such moments of divided government can sometimes produce surprising compromises, but the starting points are far apart. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, Democrats' likely next House speaker, wants to reverse the $1 trillion in healthcare cuts that Congress enacted last year as part of Trump's signature legislative package. And that's leaving aside the deep animosity between the parties. The overall U.S. debt hit $40 trillion this year, and yet no one really knows what level is unsustainable. A full-on debt crisis likely remains much further out in the future. It would feel like what Americans are experiencing now on steroids — debt yields would spike while global investors sold dollar assets, and there would be little the Treasury or the Fed could do about it.For now, though higher yields are also attracting investors to U.S. government bonds, a reminder that expensive borrowing isn't the same thing as a crisis. But the bottom line is that economics alone can't solve the problem. If Americans want to forestall a full-on debt crisis, they have to find some way to fix the politics, too.

schema.headline: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge

title: Katie Zacharia out as Trump's White House press secretary
description: watch nowNew White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her job after just five days in the face of criticism over her performance, a White
body: watch nowNew White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her job after just five days in the face of criticism over her performance, a White House official confirmed to CNBC on Friday.Earlier Friday afternoon, President Donald Trump told reporters that he had just suggested to Zacharia that she quit."I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'" Trump said outside the White House."'If I were you, I'd reconsider,'" the president said he told Zacharia.The White House official, who asked not to be named in order to discuss the staffing shake-up, confirmed Fox News' report that Zacharia is "transitioning" out of the press secretary role.Zacharia's five-day tenure in the Trump administration is shorter than that of Anthony Scaramucci, who in 2017 served as White House communications director for less than 11 days. That length of time became jokingly referred to as a "Scaramucci" and was used to measure the durations of other officials who served briefly.By that metric, Zacharia lasted one-half of one Scaramucci."Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain," Scaramucci said in an X post later Friday.Zacharia, a conservative commentator who worked at Trump Media & Technology Group, had faced widespread criticism in the days since she led a short and shaky first press briefing. She also came under mounting scrutiny about her legal background.Trump spoke to reporters before heading to Georgia for a political rally as he hopes to boost Republicans' electoral chances with just 18 days until the midterms.But Trump's efforts to sell his agenda have been muddled in part by Zacharia, who ended her first, and only, press briefing on Tuesday after delivering halting remarks and taking questions from just three reporters.In the less than six minutes she spent answering questions, Zacharia revealed that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to step down. That departure, and Zacharia's, follow those of a number of other high-ranking female officials in the Trump administration who have quit or been fired in recent months."You know, she's been treated very rough. And she's a nice person," Trump said of Zacharia outside the White House.He accused the media of treating her "very badly" and said that even Fox News TV host Sean Hannity, a supporter of the administration, was "a little bit tough" on Zacharia during her appearance on his show Thursday night.Hannity, after calling Zacharia's debut briefing "widely panned," had asked about her past claims about her legal work in light of reports that she never passed a bar exam. Zacharia has defended identifying herself as a lawyer, drawing a distinction between that label and calling herself an "attorney."Hannity pointed out that Zacharia had called herself an attorney in multiple social media posts. "I think they were retweets, and I corrected the record," she replied.Trump called Zacharia "an attorney" in his Oct. 9 Truth Social post announcing her selection to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the Trump administration in late August. Zacharia's first day was Columbus Day.White House officials had defended Zacharia earlier this week. "Up and down the White House, everyone has been thoroughly impressed with Katie in just a few short days on the job," White House communications director Steven Cheung said in an X post Wednesday. "At the end of this second term, she'll be remembered as one of the all-time greats," Cheung wrote.CNN chief White House correspondent Kaitlan Collins, however, reported Friday that Trump was "embarrassed by the coverage of Zacharia's briefing and when he polled other aides about her, Zacharia had few allies willing to stand up for her or defend her performance.""She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily," Trump said of Zacharia in Friday's remarks outside the White House. "And I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, 'Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want.'"Asked if he would keep her in the role, Trump said, "I'm going to let her make that decision."

schema.headline: Katie Zacharia out as Trump's White House press secretary

title: Nike's India campus is a long-term growth bet amid turnaround
description: A shopper carries a Nike bag in San Francisco, Dec. 17, 2025.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNike is making a big bet on India.The retaile
body: A shopper carries a Nike bag in San Francisco, Dec. 17, 2025.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNike is making a big bet on India.The retailer, which has been struggling to revive its business and regain momentum under CEO Elliott Hill, is hoping the world's most populous country can help it turn the page on its performance.As it reported its fiscal first-quarter earnings on Oct. 1, the company announced it will create a new global campus in Bengaluru, India, as part of its growth strategy. Hill wrote in a letter to employees that the new facility would be a "long-term investment" to help position Nike for success."India is already an important growth market and manufacturing hub for Nike, with strong capabilities and access to talent," Hill wrote.The new campus is expected to open in the next few years and span corporate roles across the organization, including the namesake Nike brand, Jordan Brand and Converse. Nike plans to discuss its India campus in detail at its investor day next month. In a statement to CNBC, a Nike spokesperson said expanding into India is a "natural" next step for the company as it looks to grow its global presence."As participation in running, basketball, football, fitness and other sports continues to grow across India, we see an opportunity to better serve athletes through stronger local capabilities, consumer insights, and innovation," the spokesperson said. India will be the world's third-largest retail market by 2030, according to Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries. Its e-commerce market was valued at $159.25 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach $332.94 billion by 2031, according to IBEF, a business advocacy organization created by the Indian government.Nike has endured a yearslong slump and is trying to right its business under Hill's turnaround plan. Nike also announced this month that it would lay off workers across the company as part of what it has dubbed its Pace strategy, which includes supply chain changes and reorganization of the company's geographic segments. Nike expects the effort to deliver approximately $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031. Nike's decision to invest further in India as part of its comeback comes as the sportswear company sheds revenue in another critical international market: China. Though its fiscal first-quarter North America revenue came in just above Wall Street expectations, Hill said that performance wasn't enough to offset pressures abroad.Nike has been particularly struggling in the Greater China market, where its revenue dropped by 26% in its fiscal first quarter. It's part of what experts have said is a broader trend of American companies losing relevance and traction to domestic brands as the once-lucrative market matures.On a call with analysts earlier this month, Hill said the company was taking "deliberate actions" to strengthen its China business, though he said those effects will take time to materialize. Hill said the company plans to refresh its physical retail, spearhead a digital cleanup and create higher quality experiences for consumers.The Nike spokesperson told CNBC the company is "deeply committed" to China and sees the region as one of its "most important long-term growth markets," even as Nike expands its presence in India."China remains a long-term priority for Nike, while India represents another important opportunity to invest in the future of sport and the next generation of athletes," the spokesperson said. Investing in a long-term visionThe company's expansion in India may be coming at both an opportune and inopportune time, according to experts. Investing in a growing international market does not guarantee higher sales — it also requires persuading Indian consumers they want the Nike brand, a challenge the company has struggled to overcome in China. "What Nike, I think, is doing right now is going region by region and working to reestablish what the brand stands for," Simeon Siegel, a senior managing director at Guggenheim Securities, told CNBC. Siegel said part of the dissonance for Nike is that each region and segment of the business is at a different stage of its turnaround. He said investing in India may set the company up for a more sustainable future if the China business continues to lag, but Nike needs to have a compelling product, solid storytelling and extensive distribution in the region to be successful there."I think the company needs to look inward and figure out what is the right way to reestablish profitability," he said. "And that involves, in certain instances, shrinking and saving and cutting, and, in certain instances, investing and looking toward the future, because the goal here is not to shrink to oblivion; it's to shrink to stability, and then ultimately growth."The global strategy may also focus too much on a long-term vision rather than more immediate fixes, according to Jessica Ramirez, co-founder and managing director at advisory firm The Consumer Collective, who specializes in retail and apparel. Ramirez said she already thought Nike and Hill's vision were "out of touch" and the plan for the India campus didn't necessarily help its case."I don't know that this plan of India is an immediate solution to their problems right now," she said. "They have to plan long term, right? But they also need to plan short term, which is continuously falling apart."She said Nike has not shared plans that are concrete enough to win back momentum in China and has to develop both regions hand in hand. While Nike under Hill has improved its wholesale and performance categories, Ramirez said it has yet to master its direct-to-consumer and sportswear segments, which would allow the company to flourish in all of its markets.The Nike spokesperson told CNBC the retailer is committed to investing in both countries as it tries to expand its global presence."Importantly, this is not an either/or decision between India and China," the spokesperson said. "We always invest market by market based on long-term opportunities to serve athletes and grow sport around the world."A growing market opportunityStill, India presents an attractive opportunity for many companies looking to unlock growth abroad.Ramirez said Nike is just the latest to join a cohort of American companies looking to establish their presence in the market. While many brands began investing in China years ago, she said that trend is now pointing toward India instead, as U.S. companies see more spending pressures in the Chinese market and navigate geopolitical tensions between the two countries."It's to get in there for the long term and to make sure that they are there for when they can reap the positive effects," she said. "I want to say this conversation started getting a bit more engaging in the last two to three years, when companies started investing more in India."India is one of the world's strongest market performers, driven primarily by domestic demand, investment and supply-chain diversification, according to an analysis from Accenture. With a population of over 1 billion, the country presents a growth opportunity similar to the one China offered in the early 2000s. "It's going to be a fast-growing consumer base where we assume their income levels will continue to go up and they'll have much more purchasing power, and so maybe could we be tapping in on that market from a consumer lens," Chris Tomsovic, who leads Accenture's macro foresight team, told CNBC.Still, one of the biggest focus points for the Indian consumer is price sensitivity, which will pose a challenge for American companies trying to break into the market, he added. Even so, many domestic brands on the market are younger, meaning there could be more opportunities right now for Western companies to take market share.Another challenge is that the Chinese consumer has historically been receptive to American brands, whereas it will still take more data to understand how Indian shoppers feel about those businesses, he said. For sportswear retailers, the focus of the sports most popular in each region will also factor into that equation."Can they really localize the product, make the price point work? Can they adapt to the local social media technology ecosystem? Can they adapt to the local cultural values and norms that the consumer wants?" Tomsovic said. "If you're able to nail that, then I think you're right. Whether you're a footwear brand, whether you're an athleisure brand, I think there's a huge opportunity there with a billion consumers," he said.

schema.headline: Nike's India campus is a long-term growth bet amid turnaround

title: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
description: KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has
body: KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday.Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast.The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes. "This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us."Beverage cups stacked inside a Yum Brands KFC restaurant in Shelbyville, Kentucky, Jan. 29, 2021.Luke Sharrett | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesFor many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House, its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas. Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks.KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said.Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets.For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands. It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway, the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express.

schema.headline: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades

title: Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal, praises recent global tightening
description: watch nowBANGKOK — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh refrained from signaling whether there will be another interest rate hike again this month, wh
body: watch nowBANGKOK — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh refrained from signaling whether there will be another interest rate hike again this month, while acknowledging a "synchronous tightening" by central banks around the world."I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year," Warsh said, reiterating his opposition to the use of forward guidance for markets that should rely on interpreting data. He also acknowledged that stance may disappoint anyone who had hoped for a steer ahead of the central bank meeting later this month. "It's a new chapter at the Fed [and] we're not in that business anymore," he said. Warsh spoke at a fireside chat with the International Monetary Fund's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday. "Alongside other recent comments from FOMC participants, Warsh's comments indicate that the FOMC is set to pause in October," Goldman Sachs economists led by Jan Hatzius wrote in a note. "We continue to expect a second and final hike in December."S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures edged higher following the speech, while stock market indexes in Asia and Treasury yields were largely stable.   Chair of the Federal Reserve of the United States Kevin Warsh speaks during the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group annual meetings at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center (QSNCC) in Bangkok, Thailand, on October 16, 2026.Matt Hunt | Anadolu | Getty ImagesWarsh described the global shift toward tighter monetary policy as a common fight on prices. Central banks made their own choices under their own mandates, he said, but the result was "a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world," which means "there's no free riders."Surging energy costs stemming from the Iran war and artificial intelligence investment boom are stoking inflation and pushing up borrowing costs around the world, just as global public debt is on pace to exceed 100% of the world's GDP, a level last breached in the aftermath of World War II. The U.S. government has insisted that strong growth would be the best way to grow out of its rising debt pile, dismissing IMF's warning that the plans of relying solely on growth won't work as something that needs to be taken "with a grain of salt."  Warsh also expressed optimism about how AI will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, while warning the road there may be "very bumpy," and its near-term effect on employment is still uncertain."I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose," Warsh said. A decade from now, he said, people will look back on the developments and "say this was hugely consequential." The Fed raised rates to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023. Traders see a 72.3% chance for the Fed to keep the interest rate unchanged at the Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to CME FedWatch, while the majority expect a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting.

schema.headline: Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal, praises recent global tightening

title: Here's who Netflix just brought in to run content — and what it means for the streamer
description: watch nowNetflix is shaking up its C-suite in an effort to fix its engagement woes.On Thursday, the streaming giant announced that former Disney execu
body: watch nowNetflix is shaking up its C-suite in an effort to fix its engagement woes.On Thursday, the streaming giant announced that former Disney executive Peter Rice will take over as the company's chief content officer, overseeing global content organization, including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events.Rice is replacing 10-year Netflix veteran Bela Bajaria, who most recently led the company's global content team with a focus on its live sports strategy. Bajaria was initially hired in 2016 to help the streamer launch an unscripted division as well as licensing and studio co-productions. She later transitioned to the top creative role, spearheading Netflix's $20 billion content budget.She oversaw popular TV series like "Stranger Things," "Wednesday," "Bridgerton," "Squid Game," "Adolescence" and "Beef," as well as Netflix films like "Frankenstein" and "KPop Demon Hunters." Bajaria also helped push Netflix into live sports and events, including deals with the WWE and the NFL as well as programs like "The Roast of Tom Brady."Prior to his stint at Disney, Rice was president of 21st Century Fox and CEO of Fox Networks Group as well as Fox's lead executive on the Hulu board. He was also the president of Fox Searchlight Pictures and helped release "Slumdog Millionaire," "Juno," "Little Miss Sunshine" and "Sideways."Peter Rice, seen here on May 3, 2017, was head of Disney's TV entertainment business in 2020. He was one of several executives passed over for the CEO job in favor of Chapek.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe executive change follows a tumultuous period for Netflix as it faces stagnating viewership and explores avenues for growth. It comes just days after the streaming giant laid off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce.The last time Netflix made cuts of this size was in 2022 when it reported its first quarterly subscriber loss in more than 10 years."We believe this round of layoffs reflects more structural changes to the cost base than a reaction to near-term subscriber dynamics," wrote Brian Pitz, managing director and head of internet and interactive entertainment equity research at BMO Capital Markets, in a research note published Friday.Flagging engagement In July, Netflix reported viewership increased just 2% in the first half of the year as the streamer suffers from a lack of shows with water-cooler-level hype. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted last month during the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company is "not growing as fast as I want us to." Those warnings, and now Bajaria's exit, have Wall Street bracing for more turbulence ahead. "The sudden departure of Bajaria likely signals to us that user engagement may have remained soft throughout [the third quarter]," Pitz wrote.Netflix is set to release fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday.In July, Nielsen reported that Netflix had generated 7.8% of TV viewership, while YouTube accounted for nearly double that, at 14.2%. YouTube has been Netflix's biggest threat in the battle for viewers' time. In response, the streaming giant has sought to diversify its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention."If the opportunity is to recast [Netflix] into a broader content hub, the risk is missing the watercooler originals," Steven Cahall, equity analyst at Wells Fargo, wrote in a research note last month. "We see breakout hits as a must for the stock to work again."What Rice brings to NetflixRice has a wealth of experience in television and film, most recently serving as the chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment for the company. He managed a wide swath of channels across broadcast and streaming, including ABC, Disney Channel, Hulu and FX Networks. During his tenure, he oversaw the production of more than 300 shows, including "American Idol," "Modern Family," "Abbott Elementary," "The Bear," "Only Murders in the Building" and "Shogun." He also headed up major sporting events such as coverage of the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup. Under Rice's leadership, Disney earned roughly 300 Primetime Emmy nominations between 2021 and 2022. Of those nods, it won nearly 60 awards across its television networks and streaming platforms.Meanwhile, Netflix's Emmy wins have slowed. Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesIn 2021, it tied the record for most trophies won by an outlet in a single year with 44. This year, however, it only took home 16 prizes, its lowest Emmy haul in a decade.With Rice, Netflix is also getting an executive with theatrical experience. After he was ousted by then-Disney CEO Bob Chapek in mid-2022, he transitioned into an independent producer role. Since 2023 he has produced films like "Saturday Night" and "28 Years Later." He's currently developing a movie adaptation of the video game "Elden Ring."Late last year, Netflix struck a deal to buy Warner Bros. Discovery's film studio and streaming assets, only to be outbid months later by Paramount Skydance, which completed its acquisition of WBD in early October. Some on Wall Street have speculated that the streamer may be interested in further M&A, including acquiring assets from NBCUniversal after it splits from parent company Comcast."[Rice's] long tenure at Fox, and then Disney after its acquisition of Fox, gives him unique insight into the consolidation of two major studios, relevant if Netflix chooses to go after another studio," Alicia Reese, senior vice president of equity research at Wedbush, wrote in a research note Thursday. "Even if it doesn't, Rice's experience fits well as Netflix pushes deeper into theatrical and builds a broader platform with varied content across the entertainment ecosystem."

schema.headline: Here's who Netflix just brought in to run content — and what it means for the streamer

title: Trump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in Ukraine
description: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to reporters as he departs the White House on October 16, 2026 in Washington, DC. Andrew Harnik | Getty ImagesPresi
body: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to reporters as he departs the White House on October 16, 2026 in Washington, DC. Andrew Harnik | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces.Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia.SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government."Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."Read more CNBC tech newsApple's $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the testTrump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in UkraineBlue Origin plans $330 million Florida expansion to ramp New Glenn launchesSpaceX AI policy leader grilled by NYC Council on Grok safety, sexualized imagesUkrainian forces have long relied on Starlink and Starshield to enable data gathering by their autonomous drones and for other communications. The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour.Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions." Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX."Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote. "As your European customers, we are watching you." Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian.The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions. Reuters reported on Thursday, citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order.On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far."Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday.SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. WATCH: Poland never underestimated Russia threatwatch now

schema.headline: Trump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in Ukraine

title: OpenAI Saudi national bugging case shows threat to U.S. leadership in AI: DNI Clayton
description: watch nowU.S. companies and the Trump administration both "need to be wary" of foreign espionage attempts as the race for artificial intelligence domi
body: watch nowU.S. companies and the Trump administration both "need to be wary" of foreign espionage attempts as the race for artificial intelligence dominance continues, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC on Friday.AI "amplifies" existing cybersecurity risks toward U.S. digital infrastructure, which is interconnected with critical systems related to everything from public goods to the national defense and global communications, Clayton said on "Squawk Box."It's "why we're focused on hardening those systems" and using "our commitment to continue to lead to stay ahead of those nefarious actors," said Clayton, who leads a new White House AI task force.Clayton was asked how concerned Americans should be with the threat of foreign spying in light of the recently revealed case charging Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan with allegedly installing a recording device in an OpenAI executive conference room. Alfozan has not been charged with espionage; the federal charge involves alleged interception of oral communications.Alfozan, who was an OpenAI employee, had booked a one-way plane ticket to Saudi Arabia with his wife and another family member prior to his arrest, according to federal prosecutors."The short answer to your question is espionage, both commercial espionage, and I would say state-sponsored espionage, are realities," Clayton said."It's something that our private sector companies need to be wary of. We, as a government, need to be wary of," he said. The OpenAI incident "shows the lengths that people will go to try and supplant our leadership in this, or at least stay close to us in this emerging technology," Clayton said.An ex-CIA official, who asked not to be named because they were discussing information that is not public, told CNBC this week that the case is "probably the tip of the iceberg."Clayton, who was appointed AI czar earlier this month, said that the task force's "very good" inaugural meeting at the White House on Thursday built on the accord signed by President Donald Trump and a number of AI leaders at the White House last month. Trump had described the agreement, which includes industry pledges to police AI risks itself, as "morally binding."The task force also established three subcommittees that are focused on different AI-related issues. One is tasked with reporting and response, another with assessing critical infrastructure and working with the private sector, and a third with law enforcement and responsibility, Clayton said.The DNI reiterated to CNBC that the Trump administration is intent on staying ahead in the AI race."We're not the only ones developing it. There are vectors in this technology that are coming from some of our known adversaries and competitors," he said. "The Chinese, the Russians, the Iranians, the North Koreans all have significant technical capability. We need to stay ahead of them."

schema.headline: OpenAI Saudi national bugging case shows threat to U.S. leadership in AI: DNI Clayton

title: Elon Musk cash infusion helps GOP Senate super PAC raise record $273 million
description: People walk near the U.S Capitol Building on Oct. 1, 2026 in Washington, DC. Anna Moneymaker | Getty ImagesThe Senate Leadership Fund, the Republican
body: People walk near the U.S Capitol Building on Oct. 1, 2026 in Washington, DC. Anna Moneymaker | Getty ImagesThe Senate Leadership Fund, the Republican Party's leading Senate super PAC, posted the largest quarterly haul in its history and entered the final weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm election with more than $155 million in cash, according to a new Federal Election Commission filing Thursday.The SLF brought in $272.9 million from July through September, including $209.7 million from donors — including.Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, who supplied the bulk of that moneyMusk poured $158 million into the SLF in September through an affiliated Texas PAC created to support Republican Ken Paxton. His two contributions of $75 million and $83 million are among the largest political donations ever. Musk's contribution alone also exceeded the Democratic Senate Majority PAC's entire third-quarter fundraising. That super PAC reported raising a record $151 million during the period and ended September with $111.8 million in cash, which the group said was its third-quarter record. The super PAC's FEC filings are not yet available. The SLF's haul shattered its own previous records. The group brought in nearly $116 million in the third quarter of 2024 and $111 million in 2022. In 2020, when it filed monthly reports, SLF took in roughly $157 million from July through September. Its previous quarterly high was roughly $216 million in the final three months of 2020, according to a CNBC review of FEC filings.The record influx gives Republicans a sizable financial cushion as they fight to preserve their 53-seat Senate majority across the country that has become increasingly defensive in the closing weeks of the election. The SLF paused additional advertising in perennial battleground North Carolina this month after spending more than $30 million there — according to AdImpact data — and redirected resources toward Kansas, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces an unexpectedly competitive challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton.In Nebraska, SLF has committed $15 million to defend Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, including $7 million through the affiliated Cornhusker Majority, The Wall Street Journal reported this week. Trump carried Nebraska by more than 20 percentage points in 2024.The super PAC has also been central to the Republican intervention in Texas, where Democrat James Talarico has turned what had been expected to be a safe GOP Senate contest into one of the most expensive races in the country.Republican groups spent roughly $122 million in Texas in September alone and had another $66 million in advertising reserved through Election Day as of the beginning of October, according to AdImpact data. Talarico announced Thursday that he raised $64 million in the third quarter, the largest third-quarter haul on record for a Senate candidate. Paxton raised $10.2 million, according to a FEC filing.

schema.headline: Elon Musk cash infusion helps GOP Senate super PAC raise record $273 million

title: Blue Origin plans $330 million Florida expansion to ramp New Glenn launches
description: watch nowJeff Bezos' Blue Origin said Friday it plans to make extensive upgrades to its Florida launch facilities with the goal of supporting multiple
body: watch nowJeff Bezos' Blue Origin said Friday it plans to make extensive upgrades to its Florida launch facilities with the goal of supporting multiple flights per week by the end of the decade.The company will add two more launch and landing pads for New Glenn, its heavy-lift, partially reusable rocket. A $330 million expansion to its Rocket Park campus in Cape Canaveral, expected to be complete in the summer of 2027, will enable it to produce up to 150 upper stages of its New Glenn rocket annually, Blue Origin said in a blog post. "These investments are centered on one goal: building the capacity to support more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently," Ian Richardson, Blue Origin's senior vice president of operations, wrote in the post. "As we look ahead, this infrastructure is designed to support multiple flights per week by the end of the decade." Blue Origin is working to ramp up its launch cadence as it vies to compete with its chief rival, Elon Musk's SpaceX, for commercial and government customers. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp told CNBC's Morgan Brennan last month that the company's first outside funding round is "oversubscribed." The company had raised $10 billion for the round, valuing it at $140 billion, The Wall Street Journal reported. The company is also recovering from a setback in May, when one of its New Glenn rockets exploded on the launchpad. Blue Origin has been aggressively restoring the launchpad with a goal of returning New Glenn to flight by the end of 2026. As part of the upgrades, Blue Origin said it's building a new customer integration facility with the U.S. Space Force at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station that will enable it to "prepare multiple missions at once" when it's up and running.Blue Origin has invested more than $3 billion in its infrastructure and facilities in Florida, which now spans more than 20 sites across the state's Brevard and Orange counties, with more than 5,000 employees, Richardson said. The space industry is also grappling with a launch capacity shortage, as SpaceX has stopped offering commercial rides on its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket to prioritize its massive Starship rocket. That's spurred a flurry of investment, with $92.5 billion invested in the commercial space sector in the first three quarters of 2026, according to a report this week by venture capital firm Space Capital. Blue Origin, SpaceX and other rocket providers are seeing increasing demand from companies and governments trying to deploy satellites into orbit. Both Blue Origin and SpaceX have their own satellite internet services, and they're launch partners for Amazon, which is in the process of standing up its full Leo low Earth orbit satellite constellation. SpaceX's Starlink currently dominates the market with more than 11,000 satellites in orbit.Read more CNBC tech newsApple's $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the testTrump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in UkraineBlue Origin plans $330 million Florida expansion to ramp New Glenn launchesSpaceX AI policy leader grilled by NYC Council on Grok safety, sexualized images

title: Norway's $2 trillion wealth fund was frozen out of major defense companies. That may be about to change
description: A BAE Systems Hawk T1 jet, pictured Sept. 20, 2026. BAE Systems has been excluded from NBIM's fund since 2018. Artur Widak | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesNo
body: A BAE Systems Hawk T1 jet, pictured Sept. 20, 2026. BAE Systems has been excluded from NBIM's fund since 2018. Artur Widak | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesNorway's $2.3 trillion oil fund could soon invest in Western defense companies after years of being frozen out of much of the sector by state ethics guidelines.The sovereign wealth fund is currently worth around 21.8 trillion Norwegian kroner, or $2.3 trillion, making it the largest fund of its kind in the world. With stakes in around 1.5% of the world's publicly listed companies, the fund is one of the biggest investors in the stock market worldwide. In November 2025, a review was ordered into the ethical guidelines governing how Norges Bank invests, following controversy over divestments from some Israeli and American firms. On Thursday, the independent Gjedrem Committee submitted the review's findings to the Norwegian Ministry of Finance. It included a recommendation for radical change to the fund's approach to defense investments, arguing that "Norges Bank must be prepared for situations where conflicts escalate into war."Current ethical rules prohibit the fund from making investments in companies including Airbus, BAE Systems, Boeing, BWX Technologies and Lockheed Martin, as they contribute to the manufacturing of nuclear weapons. The fund does hold some defense stocks, including a 2.3% stake in Germany's Rheinmetall, and a 1.5% stake in Italy's Leonardo.The Gjedrem Committee said Thursday that although the nuclear weapons criterion should be retained, "its scope should change.""The Fund is not to be invested in companies that produce nuclear weapons, unless the company is domiciled in a nuclear-weapon state under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) that is allied with Norway," it said in its report. "Several European and American companies that produce components for nuclear weapons can therefore be reincluded."It added that potential investment should include companies producing weapons that Norway needs for its own defense, and proposed removing the requirement for arms-makers to be assessed for whether their products are being used by nations in accordance with international humanitarian law.The committee noted that alongside rising geopolitical instability, wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, and energy security concerns, the fund's capital and influence meant it was "timely to reassess the ethical framework.""The Fund's size and reach give better access to company management and boards than the Fund had in 2003," it said. "In a time of a more demanding political situation abroad, this provides opportunities of which the management should make use.""The liberal, rules-based international order is in decline," it added. "Economic policies are increasingly used as instruments of foreign policy. Cooperation between countries has become more transactional and negotiation-driven in recent years."It warned that in this environment, other governments can "more readily perceive ethically motivated exclusions as the policy of the Norwegian government."Norway's oil fund was set up in the 1990s to invest revenues from the country's oil and gas industry. While Norway's finance ministry and central bank are involved in the governance of the fund, investment decisions are made by Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), with exclusion recommendations historically put forward by its independent Council on Ethics. "There have been reactions and threats of countermeasures," the Gjedrem Committee said in its report on Thursday. "Retaliatory measures could hit the Fund and other Norwegian interests."U.S. backlash In September last year, the U.S. State Department told CNBC it was "very troubled" by NBIM's decision to exit positions in American machinery manufacturer Caterpillar and five Israeli banks, accusing the fund of basing its decision on "illegitimate claims."NBIM had cited "unacceptable risk" that the companies were contributing to rights violations in Palestinian territories when it divested. Norway's finance minister, Jens Stoltenberg – former secretary general of NATO – said at the time that it was "not a political decision."The Gjedrem Committee noted on Thursday that the risk of further backlash to NBIM's investment choices was also rising as public finances came under greater pressure in many countries."High government debt can jeopardize economic stability in countries, but can also give an incentive to look to foreign investors' interest and dividend income as a revenue base for the state," it warned. The committee members concluded that although the guidelines underpinning the fund's ethical framework still have broad support, they had come under pressure against the political backdrop. "The conditions for exercising ownership have become more restrictive, in the U.S. among other places," they said. The Gjedrem Committee recommended that the Council on Ethics should continue to operate, but that it should no longer advise NBIM on taking action over ethical concerns. Instead, it should be limited to delivering analysis on breaches of the ethical guidelines by companies, the committee added.No new companies will immediately be included in or excluded from the fund's portfolio as a result of the report's recommendations – but the recommendations pave the way for the fund to invest in some American and European defense companies that are currently barred under the fund's ethics rules.Norway will now hold a public consultation on the recommendations made in the report, with the central bank due to submit its response in January. The finance ministry will propose a new ethics framework in a white paper in the spring, with Norway's parliament expected to vote on the changes in mid-2027. Until then, the fund's current ethical guidelines and exclusion framework remain unchanged. "The Council on Ethics has just received the Gjedrem Committee's report," Svein Richard Brandtzæg, chair of the wealth fund's Council on Ethics, said in an emailed statement on Thursday morning. "We will study the report carefully. We will then hold thorough discussions within the Council and submit our response in the upcoming public consultation."Until November 2025, the Executive Board of Norges Bank decided whether companies should be excluded from the fund's investment portfolio or placed on an observation list. These decisions were informed by the Council on Ethics, an independent body appointed by Norway's Ministry of Finance.But, pending the Gjedrem Committee's review, temporary guidelines were put in place, under which Norges Bank could no longer make those decisions. The temporary guidelines stipulated that the board may only revoke previous decisions on excluding a company or putting it on the observation list. Meanwhile, the Council on Ethics was stripped of its ability to recommend observation or exclusion at least until the ethical framework review is finalized.The temporary guidelines will remain in place until the 2027 parliamentary vote on the Gjedrem Committee's review. 'Other investors pay attention'The Gjedrem Committee's report was met with backlash from some human rights groups, who argued decisions made in Norway could have implications for international investment trends. John Peder Egenæs, secretary general of Amnesty International Norway, said in a statement on Thursday that the proposals "risk weakening accountability and integrity and dismantling key human rights protections.""When the world's largest sovereign wealth fund changes its standards, the consequences do not stop at Norway's borders," he said. "Other investors pay attention, and companies do too."Grete Herlofson, secretary general of the Norwegian Red Cross, said in a statement that investing in producers of nuclear weapons would be "ethically and humanitarianly completely incomprehensible.""Opening up investment in nuclear weapons would be a dangerous change of course that weakens the international stigma against these weapons and reinforces the perception that they are an acceptable weapon," she said. "This increases the risk that they could be used."

schema.headline: Norway's $2 trillion wealth fund was frozen out of major defense companies. That may be about to change
